pos: adv. (craftily, by guile; in a wily manner)
etymology: From wily, from wile, a trick or stratagem, probably from Old Norse vel, craft, with the adverbial -ly. The Hebrew ormah means craftiness or subtilty, the same word used of the serpent's subtilty in Genesis 3.
biblical_def: The Gibeonites, hearing what Israel had done to Jericho and Ai, save themselves by a lie: “They did work wilily, and went and made as if they had been ambassadors, and took old sacks upon their asses, and wine bottles, old, and rent, and bound up” (Joshua 9:4). To work wilily is to work by guile, and the staging was thorough: worn sacks, cracked bottles, mouldy bread, the whole costume of men who had travelled far. Israel inspected the props and made a league, and the one thing they did not do was ask counsel at the mouth of the LORD. The result bound Israel by oath to a people they had been commanded to destroy, and the oath was honoured, as Joshua's successors learned when Saul broke it centuries later and the land suffered famine. Guile is not always sinful in Scripture — the Lord Himself sends His people out “wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew 10:16) — but guile against the covenant people is always met in the end by the God who sees it: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): WILILY, by stratagem; craftily; cunningly; WILE, a trick or stratagem practiced for ensnaring.
webster_full: WILILY, adv. By stratagem; craftily; cunningly; with insidious art.
WILE, n. A trick or stratagem practiced for ensnaring or deception.
WILY, a. Cunning; sly; using craft or stratagem to accomplish a purpose.
Hebrew ormah, craftiness or subtilty, as of the serpent in Genesis 3.

Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Eph 6:11

corruption_summary: Spiritual deception is expected to arrive looking wicked, so that a deceit dressed in the props of poverty and piety is examined by eye and never taken to prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Joshua 9 teaches by Israel's failure: a deceit prepared well enough will pass visual inspection, and the only defence is to ask counsel at the mouth of the LORD.

Israel did examine the evidence. The sacks were old, the bottles were split, the bread was dry; everything checked out, and they made the league. What they omitted was prayer, and the text names the omission as the hinge of the whole disaster. The modern church makes the same mistake with its own due diligence: references checked, credentials verified, orthodoxy professed, and no serious seeking of God. The wiles of the devil are never crude enough to be caught by eye alone.

etymology: From shameless, from shame, Old English sceamu, with -less and -ly. The Hebrew phrase in 2 Samuel 6:20 uses galah, to uncover, with the sense of exposing oneself without regard.
biblical_def: When David brings the ark into Jerusalem dancing before the LORD, his wife meets him at the door with contempt: “Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself!” (2 Samuel 6:20). Shamelessly means without shame, brazenly, and Michal's charge is that the king had behaved like a commoner and lost his dignity. David's answer refuses her whole standard: “It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD” (2 Samuel 6:21). The narrative then records that Michal had no child unto the day of her death. The word is therefore worth careful handling. Michal uses it of David wrongly; there is a real shamelessness, and Scripture condemns it severely. But a king who humbles himself before God is not shameless, and the pattern is perfected in One “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2).

webster_full: SHAMELESSLY, adv. Without shame; impudently; audaciously.
SHAMELESS, a. Destitute of shame; wanting modesty; impudent; brazen-faced.
SHAME, n. A painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt or impropriety.
Hebrew galah, to uncover or expose.

scriptures: Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself!

And David said unto Michal, It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD.
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
corruption_summary: Shame is treated as always an injury to be healed, so that the shame Scripture calls proper is abolished along with the shame that is false.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic teaching has made shame a single category and that category wholly bad: shame is said to be the wound beneath every sin and the thing from which people must be freed. Scripture is more careful. There is a false shame, which Michal urges on David and which the gospel destroys, and a proper shame, which Scripture repeatedly commands the sinner to feel — were they ashamed? nay, they were not at all ashamed, is said as an indictment, not a diagnosis.

The distinction runs on what the shame is about. David had nothing to be ashamed of in dancing before the ark, and his answer is not self-defence but a confession of whose he is. The vain fellow who uncovers himself in the street has everything to be ashamed of, and the loss of that capacity is itself a judgment. And at the centre of the gospel is a Saviour who took upon Himself the shame that was properly ours, despising it for the joy set before Him, so that the believer's shame is covered rather than merely renamed.

etymology: From unfaithful, from faith, Latin fides, with un-, -ful and -ly. The Hebrew bagad means to act treacherously, to deal falsely with a covenant partner.
biblical_def: The long historical psalm of Asaph reaches the generation of the judges and gives its verdict: “But turned back, and dealt unfaithfully like their fathers: they were turned aside like a deceitful bow” (Psalm 78:57). To deal unfaithfully is to deal treacherously, to break faith with one to whom faith is owed. The Hebrew bagad is covenant language; this is not general wickedness but betrayal of a relationship, and Asaph makes the point sharper with his figure. A deceitful bow is one whose warp sends the arrow aside: aimed rightly, drawn fully, and still missing. Israel did not become irreligious; she kept shooting, and the shot went wide. The psalm has already named the ancestral pattern: “And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God” (Psalm 78:8). Against that whole history stands the one faithfulness that never warps: “They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). Covenant rests on God's fidelity, not on ours; which is the only reason any covenant survives.

webster_full: UNFAITHFULLY, adv. In a manner not to be trusted; treacherously; perfidiously.

corruption_summary: Covenant unfaithfulness is reduced to inconsistency or poor habits, a matter of self-management rather than of treachery against a Person.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious vocabulary has almost no word for treachery. Sin is described as inconsistency, as a lapse in discipline, as a pattern to be addressed; the language is drawn from habit-formation and self-improvement and it is addressed to no one. Asaph's word is relational and severe: they dealt unfaithfully, they broke faith, they betrayed a covenant partner.

Nothing is gained by softening it, and much is lost. If sin is only inconsistency, repentance is only a resolution; if sin is treachery, repentance is reconciliation with a wronged Person. And the comfort lies on the same axis. A people whose covenant rested on their own steadiness would have been destroyed in the generation Psalm 78 describes. The reason they were not is the faithfulness that is new every morning, and the reason believers are not is the same.

pos: adv. (in an unrighteous manner; wrongfully, unjustly)
etymology: From unrighteous, from right, Old English riht, with un-, -ous and -ly. The Hebrew evel means injustice or wrong, especially fraud in weights and measures.
biblical_def: The law of honest weights ends with a sweeping verdict: “For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 25:16). The immediate subject is commercial fraud, the two sets of weights a merchant kept in his bag, one for buying and one for selling. The positive command stands just before it: “But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Deuteronomy 25:15). What startles in verse 16 is the category: a shaved weight is called an abomination, the word used of idolatry and of the sins that drove out the Canaanites. God does not keep a lesser vocabulary for commercial sins. Solomon says the same in a line: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). And the law's reach is wider than the scale: all that do unrighteously takes in the employer, the contractor, the landlord and the clerk. Honest measure is not a lesser holiness.

webster_full: UNRIGHTEOUSLY, adv. Unjustly; wickedly; sinfully.

corruption_summary: Private piety is separated from commercial honesty, so that a man may be sound in doctrine and devotion while keeping two sets of weights in his bag.
corruption_paragraphs: A long-standing failure of conservative religion is the quarantining of business from worship. Doctrine is guarded, the sabbath kept, the family catechised, and the ledger left alone; sharp practice is called shrewdness, and the law of honest weight is treated as a lesser commandment than the ones that govern belief.

Scripture puts the shaved weight in the same category as the idol. Deuteronomy calls it abomination; Proverbs says a just weight is the LORD's delight; Amos indicts a nation for making the ephah small and the shekel great; Micah asks whether God shall count them pure with the bag of deceitful weights. The clause all that do unrighteously reaches past the scale to every contract, invoice and wage. A man's measures are a doctrine of God: they say what he believes about the One who sees them.

pos: adv. (basely; in a manner showing contempt, shamefully)
etymology: From vile, Old French vil, from Latin vilis, cheap, of little worth, with the adverbial -ly. The Hebrew gaal means to defile or treat as foul.
biblical_def: David's lament over Saul and Jonathan curses the mountain where they fell: “Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew, neither let there be rain, upon you, nor fields of offerings: for there the shield of the mighty is vilely cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil” (2 Samuel 1:21). To be vilely cast away is to be thrown aside as worthless. The shield of a king, the emblem of Israel's defence, lay abandoned on a hillside like refuse, and David's grief fastens on the dishonour of it: as though he had not been anointed with oil. What is remarkable is who is speaking. Saul had hunted David for years, and David had twice spared him. Now the man with every reason for satisfaction composes a public lament, forbids rejoicing in Gath and Askelon, and calls Saul the beauty of Israel: “The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!” (2 Samuel 1:19). The song ends where it began: “How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!” (2 Samuel 1:27). Grief for the fall of the LORD's anointed, even an enemy, is a mark of a godly man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VILELY, basely; meanly; shamefully; VILE, base; mean; worthless; despicable.
webster_full: VILELY, adv. Basely; meanly; shamefully.

corruption_summary: The fall of an enemy is received with satisfaction and published as vindication, where David composed a lament and forbade his people to rejoice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is David's conduct over the body of the man who had hunted him: he mourned, he honoured the office, he suppressed the news in Philistine streets, and he had the lament taught to the children of Judah.

The temptation is strongest where the enmity was real. A rival discredited, an opponent exposed, a persecutor fallen: the flesh calls this vindication and wants it broadcast. Scripture forbids it. Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, says Proverbs, lest the LORD see it and turn away His wrath from him. David's song over Gilboa is the practical shape of loving an enemy, written by a man who had every human warrant for the opposite.

pos: adv. (perversely; in a wayward, contrary manner)
etymology: From froward, Old English fromweard, turned away, from from and -ward; the exact opposite of toward. The Hebrew shobab means backsliding or turning away.
biblical_def: In the middle of Isaiah's indictment of covetous Israel comes a sentence of extraordinary weight: “For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart” (Isaiah 57:17). To go frowardly is to go perversely; the old English word means literally turned away, the precise opposite of toward. Three divine acts are named — wrath, smiting, hiding — and the man's response to all three is to keep walking in the direction he had chosen. Chastening by itself does not convert; a hidden God does not by itself humble. And then the verse that follows is one of the most unexpected in the prophets: “I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners” (Isaiah 57:18). The same eyes that saw the froward walk pronounce healing. Grace is not drawn out by improvement; it interrupts. Solomon gives the practical charge: “Put away from thee a froward mouth, and perverse lips put far from thee” (Proverbs 4:24).

webster_full: FROWARDLY, adv. Perversely; in a peevish manner.

corruption_summary: Hardness under chastening is explained as a psychological defence rather than perversity of will, which removes both the guilt and the need of a sovereign work of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern pastoral vocabulary accounts for the unmoved sinner in terms of defence mechanisms, woundedness and coping strategies. Something real is often being described; affliction does harden people, and the sufferer's history matters. But the therapeutic account cannot name what Isaiah names, which is a will turned away, walking on in the way of his heart while God is wroth and hidden.

The dictionary holds total depravity: the fall reaches the will, so that chastening alone cannot bend it. That is exactly why Isaiah 57:18 is gospel. God does not say, now that he is sorry I will heal him; He says, I have seen his ways, and will heal him. The froward man is healed by a sovereign and effectual mercy that comes down to him in his frowardness. Lose the diagnosis and that sentence becomes a platitude; keep it, and the verse is salvation.

pos: n. pl. (luxuries; costly refinements of food and living)
etymology: From delicacy, from Latin delicatus, giving pleasure, dainty, related to deliciae, delights. The Greek strenos means wanton luxury, insolent excess, and occurs only here in the New Testament.
biblical_def: The angel announcing Babylon's fall names the sin of the merchants who grew rich on her: “For all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth are waxed rich through the abundance of her delicacies” (Revelation 18:3). The Greek strenos behind delicacies is stronger than the English suggests: it means wanton luxury, the insolence of excess. Babylon is not condemned for being wealthy but for a self-glorifying softness that trades in appetite and makes others rich by feeding it. Her own words are quoted: “How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her: for she saith in her heart, I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow” (Revelation 18:7). The same pattern is drawn in a single man by our Lord: “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day” (Luke 16:19) — and Lazarus lay at his gate. Luxury is judged not by its cost but by what it makes a man blind to.

webster_full: DELICACY, n. Any thing that gratifies a nice taste; a dainty; as the delicacies of the table.

corruption_summary: Luxury is defended as the reward of diligence or condemned as wealth itself, when Scripture indicts the self-glorifying softness that cannot see the beggar at the gate.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel reads comfort as evidence of divine approval and answers every warning about luxury by pointing to Abraham's herds and Solomon's gold. On that account Revelation 18 cannot indict anybody who tithes. The opposite error, pressed by liberation readings, treats wealth as such as the sin and turns the chapter into an economic manifesto.

John gives the actual charge in Babylon's own words: I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow. The sin is a softness that has made itself invulnerable, glorified itself, and lost the capacity to imagine loss or notice need. Christ draws the same portrait at the scale of one man: purple and fine linen, faring sumptuously every day, and a beggar at the gate he never saw. Delicacies are judged by their fruit in a soul, not by their price.

pos: n. (daintiness; the softness bred by sheltered luxury)
etymology: From delicate, Latin delicatus, dainty, pampered, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew anag means to be soft or pampered, to be delicately bred.
biblical_def: Among the curses of Deuteronomy 28 is one that reaches the most sheltered woman in Israel: “The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom, and toward her son, and toward her daughter” (Deuteronomy 28:56). Delicateness is the softness bred by shelter and plenty, so complete that this woman will not set a bare foot on the earth. The curse does not merely take away her comfort; it shows what the comfort had concealed. Under siege her eye turns evil toward husband and children, and the next verse names the horror that follows. The chapter has already given the ground of the whole judgment: “Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things” (Deuteronomy 28:47), and “all these curses shall come upon thee... because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 28:45). Ingratitude in plenty is the sin; the stripping away of delicateness is the sentence; and what is exposed beneath it was there all along.

corruption_summary: The covenant curses are read as evidence of a cruel God, and the chapter's stated cause — ingratitude in the midst of abundance — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28 is among the most frequently cited chapters in the case against the God of the Old Testament, and the siege horrors of verses 53 to 57 are the exhibits. The objection assumes that the curses are arbitrary cruelty. The chapter itself gives the cause twice over: Israel would not serve the LORD with joyfulness and gladness of heart for the abundance of all things, and would not hearken to His voice. These are covenant sanctions, published in advance, accepted by the people, and inflicted after centuries of warning by prophets.

There is a second and quieter error, common among believers: reading the chapter as being about other, harder people. The verse chooses the most sheltered woman in Israel precisely to forestall that. Delicateness is not innocence; it is a covering. Under pressure her eye turns evil toward her own household. The right use of the passage is self-examination in plenty, and gratitude while gratitude is easy.

pos: n. pl. (female relatives; women related by blood)
etymology: A compound of kin, Old English cynn, family or kind, and women. Kinswoman is the feminine of kinsman. The Hebrew shaarah denotes near kindred, flesh-relation.
biblical_def: The laws of forbidden degrees in Leviticus 18 use the word once, closing a particular door: “Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness” (Leviticus 18:17). Kinswomen are female blood relatives, and the reason given is the relation itself: they are her near kinswomen. The chapter's governing principle is stated at its head: “None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 18:6). What makes these unions wicked is not social convention but the creational structure of the family, and God signs each section with His own name. The chapter closes with the reason Israel must differ from the nations around her: “Therefore shall ye keep mine ordinance, that ye commit not any one of these abominable customs, which were committed before you, and that ye defile not yourselves therein: I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 18:30). The household is the first institution God made, and He guards its boundaries Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): KINSWOMAN, a female relation; KIN, relation, properly by consanguinity or blood.
webster_full: KINSWOMAN, n. A female relation.
KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
KIN, n. Relation, properly by consanguinity or blood; kindred.
Hebrew shaarah, near kindred or flesh-relation.
Leviticus 18:17 forbids these unions because they are her near kinswomen.
scriptures: Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.
Lev 18:6

corruption_summary: Sexual boundaries are made a matter of consent and cultural convention, so that a prohibition God grounds in kinship is treated as an ancient taboo with no claim on the present.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing sexual ethic of the age is consent between adults, with everything else held to be inherited taboo. On that account Leviticus 18 is a survival from a world of tribal purity codes and binds nobody; and the argument is pressed consistently, since the same reasoning that retires these verses retires the ones before and after them.

Scripture grounds the prohibitions in creation and in the nature of God, not in custom. The reason given is kinship itself — they are her near kinswomen — and the chapter is punctuated with I am the LORD. Christ confirms the creational pattern by going back to the beginning, male and female, one flesh; and Paul applies Leviticus' own logic to a Corinthian case of incest and demands discipline. Marriage between one man and one woman, outside the forbidden degrees, remains the only legitimate category of sexual union, because the God who made the family said so.
roots_summary: Kin plus women; Hebrew shaarah, near kindred; Leviticus 18:17 forbids these unions because they are near kinswomen.
roots_lines: Old English cynn, family or kind, gives kin, kinsman and kinswoman.
Hebrew shaarah, near kindred or flesh-relation.
Leviticus 18:17 is the only occurrence of kinswomen in the Authorized Version.
The reason given is the kinship itself, not social convention.
Each section of the chapter is signed, I am the LORD.
usage: for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness
names the blood relation that makes the union wicked

pos: adj. (archaic; vigorous, robust, in full bodily strength)
etymology: From lust, Old English lust, which originally meant pleasure, desire or vigour without moral reproach, with the adjectival -y. The Hebrew shamen means fat, stout or well-fed, hence robust. The modern sexual connotation is a later narrowing.
biblical_def: After Ehud's blow fell on Eglon, Israel came down to the fords of Jordan: “And they slew of Moab at that time about ten thousand men, all lusty, and all men of valour; and there escaped not a man” (Judges 3:29). Lusty here means robust, vigorous, in full bodily strength, and the word carries no sexual freight whatever in 1611 English; the Hebrew means stout or well-fed. The verse is a careful piece of reporting: Moab's fallen were not a rabble but ten thousand strong and able men, and not one escaped. The point is where the victory came from. Israel's deliverer had been a left-handed man with a homemade dagger, sent after eighteen years of servitude in answer to a cry; and the result was that “Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest fourscore years” (Judges 3:30). The psalmist states the doctrine behind it: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength” (Psalm 33:16). Ten thousand lusty men are no defence against the LORD.

webster_full: LUSTY, a. Stout; vigorous; robust; healthful; able of body.

Judges 3:29 says the ten thousand of Moab were all lusty, and all men of valour.

corruption_summary: A word that meant bodily vigour in 1611 is read with its modern sexual sense, and the reader concludes that the Authorized Version says something it does not.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition in the doctrinal sense, but it illustrates a real hazard in reading an older English Bible. Lusty in Judges 3:29 means stout and able-bodied; the modern reader hears a sexual word and silently rewrites the verse. The same trap waits at conversation meaning manner of life, prevent meaning go before, let meaning hinder, and charity meaning love.

The principle to recover is that a Bible in older English must be read with attention to older English, not with an assumed modern dictionary. This is not an argument against the Authorized Version but for careful reading of it: Webster, a good concordance and the margin resolve nearly every case. And the verse read rightly preaches well: ten thousand robust and valiant men fell before a deliverer God raised up, because no mighty man is delivered by much strength.
roots_summary: From lust in its old sense of vigour; Hebrew shamen, stout or well-fed; Judges 3:29 calls Moab's ten thousand all lusty.
